Thanks again for the pointer towards the uv rect and the clipping in the `DCLayerTree`!

I've debugged this further. There are two issues that cause the artifacts:

**Issue 1**

The [code](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:components/viz/service/display/display.cc;l=1053-1062;drc=cdf3ed32a94019461b37aa1f4a517847eb0989da) before `DirectRenderer::DrawFrame()` resizes the root render pass to match the size of the viewport if the root render pass is smaller than the viewport. That can make the frame larger and adds a gutter where nothing is being painted. When we use viewporter, it shows stale pixels in that area. Without viewporter, it shows black pixels (which the authors of that code thought was acceptable). A simple fix for the stale pixels is to resize the viewport instead of the frame when we use viewporter. I fixed this in crrev.com/c/7156576.

**Issue 2**

This is a race condition.

When our code tries to get a frame shown on screen, it first [calls](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:gpu/command_buffer/service/shared_image/dxgi_swap_chain_image_backing.cc;l=283;drc=92e802d8fa66bafb0cca9ed32143d6148d8e0411) `Present()` on the swap chain and then [calls](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:ui/gl/dc_layer_tree.cc;l=1034;drc=35d26d364efb57d0386b98312ba739f7f65ae97e) `Commit()` on the DComp device.

Thank you, Avi and Charlie, for the thorough analysis and for taking the time to investigate this issue.

After reviewing your comments, I traced the root cause again to Edge's asynchronous browser destruction for our "Clear Browsing Data on Exit" feature. The `OnWindowClosing_EdgeMaybeClearBrowsingDataOnLastBrowserCloseForProfile()` method can delay browser destruction via an async callback, which creates a window where context menu cleanup occurs during WebContents destruction. Chrome's synchronous `OnWindowClosing()` doesn't have this issue.

I've abandoned this CL and created an Edge-side fix instead, I am considering adding an early-exit check in `send_tab_to_self::ShowBubble()` when the WebContents is being destroyed.

Thank you again for pointing me in the right direction. I'll be more careful to investigate Edge-specific divergences before submitting upstream CLs in the future.

Thank you very much for the review. Your comment about placing the eager-removal closer to where animations are added made me reconsider the approach. The fix now applies to all animations not just transitions.

TLDR: Instead of handling this in css_animations.cc for transitions specifically, the removal belongs more generally in Animation::cancel() itself, and PlayInternal() re-adds the animation if it is later replayed.

Longer version: The per-element Animations() set is currently only explicitly modified by KeyframeEffect::AttachTarget() (insert) and KeyframeEffect::DetachTarget() (erase). Every time these are called, the callers also update effect_target_ accordingly. Set membership and effect target always move together. As a consequence, the element's Animations() set is equivalent to "all animations whose effect target points to this element." This equivalence also holds for cancelled animations, which causes dead weight for consumers because cancelled animations are inert (consumers actually have guards preventing idle animations from having effect) and the tests show that this can be expensive.

The existing test CanceledTriggeredAnimationGarbageCollected demonstrates this directly. After calling cancel(), the test asserts the animation is still in the set, and only after garbage collection, when the WeakMember reference is swept, does it assert removal. The old code relied entirely on GC to clean up cancelled animations.

It probably looks like this was a wrong assumption that introduced a bunch of unnecessary exit-synchronization complexity just to manage run_nesting_level_.

A closer breakpointing of this class reveals that Run() which manages run_nesting_level_ state is never actually executed for OS-driven loops like the iOS main thread, so there is no need to set run_nesting_level_ for pre-existing loops in OnAttach() at all.

Leaving run_nesting_level_ alone completely eliminates the exit-synchronization block and simplifies the logic.

The entire change is now down to two clean parts:

(1) OnAttach() pushes placeholder frames to match the pre-existing host nesting depth.
(2) The OS observer naturally pops them as the nested loops unwind. No changes needed here.

That insight was spot on. Thanks!

Thank you, Scott! That matches our observation as well: `obscuredContentInsets` by itself adjusts the CSS viewport units (`svh`, `dvh`, `lvh`) and fixed/sticky element positioning, while `UIScrollView.contentInset` controls the native scroll view padding.

To share a bit more context on why we need this direct pass-through on `CWVWebView`: in the iGA, we use both `WKWebView` and `CWVWebView` behind a shared protocol (`GMOWebViewProtocol`) rather than branching on the concrete web view type. Through that protocol, the host application already manages `scrollView.contentInset` and `obscuredContentInsets` directly and identically for both web view implementations. Exposing `obscuredContentInsets` directly on `CWVWebView` (without `CRWWebViewContentView` also mutating `scrollView.contentInset` or `contentInsetAdjustmentBehavior` under the hood) lets `CWVWebView` conform to our shared protocol with the exact same behavior and expectations.

We've also updated `crw_web_view_proxy.h` in Patchset 6 to place `obscuredInsets` and `obscuredContentInsets` next to each other and clearly document the difference between the two (and ensured in `CRWWebController` `didFinishNavigation:` that `obscuredContentInsets` is applied after `mimeType` updates so it isn't reset). 8427086/73aece40_0d5c03d8.text:
Yes, it's the computed value. That's on purpose, since the code that creates the markers and the group also checks the computed value (`StyleRecalcContext::FromParentContext()` and `ComputedStyle::CanGeneratePseudoElement()`), so they should agree.

I double-checked your case and it's a good catch. Layout picks a marker's group with the used value (`LayoutObject::IsScrollContainer()`), so layout and this check disagree for a propagating body.

So if `html` and `body` both have a `scroll-marker-group` and body has `overflow: auto`, setting `html { overflow: clip }` makes body a scroller in layout without changing its style. In release that hangs the tab, because `PopulateScrollMarkerGroup()` loops forever.

It happens without this CL too. I'll file a separate bug for it so this CL stays focused, if that makes sense 🙂

Good catch on the unit test. In production, CriticalUserJourneyService (critical_user_journey_service.cc, which wasn't in this diff) handles Step 0 detection: Initialize() inspects journey->steps()[0] (including looping over trigger_step->branches if Step 0 is an AddAnyOf subsequence, as in ReadAnythingJourney and ClearBrowsingHistoryJourney) and RegisterJourneyTrigger() subscribes to ElementTracker for the specific event (Shown, Activated, or CustomEvent in any context) before calling session->Start(metric_id, element). In CriticalUserJourneySessionTest, session->Start() is called directly without CriticalUserJourneyService, so in Patch Set 4 I updated StepInAnyContextMatchesDifferentElementContext to call el1.Activate() and added a CHECK in BuildSequence() that initial_element->identifier() == trigger_step->id when an element ID is specified.

I really like the idea of pre-building a standby sequence in a waiting slot and rotating a new one in when Step 0's StartCallback fires so CriticalUserJourneyService doesn't have to manage ElementTracker subscriptions separately. I had Jetski help me trace how that would work with InteractionSequence, and the main thing we'd need to account for is that CriticalUserJourneyService initializes at Profile startup before a browser window ElementContext is known (whereas session->Start() currently binds builder.SetContext(element->context()) from Step 0's matched element so subsequent ContextMode::kInitial steps stay scoped to that window,
